instance: `kubectl patch`/`kubectl replace` on a k8s Secret managed by ExternalSecrets Operator (ESO) silently succeeds (rc=0, resourceVersion bumps) but ESO reconciles the change back within seconds — observed on `fleet-dispatch-tokens` in `ai-fleet`. instance: A terminal SUCCESS signal was treated as proof the work succeeded. A fleet-dispatch `impl-grok` review task was enqueued, the Grok consumer claimed the lease (`lease_holder: grok`) and reported `state: done` — and that was announced as "fully wired, end-to-end confirmed." But the job produced nothing usable: the consumer never injected the referenced GitHub issue body (Grok's own reasoning said "I need to find what article they're referring to"), the stored result was truncated to exactly **1024 bytes** of opening reasoning, and no comment was mirrored to the issue. `done` described the queue lifecycle, not the deliverable (2026-06-18).
check: Never accept a terminal/OK status (`done`, rc=0, HTTP 200, lease-claimed, "tests pass") as evidence the work succeeded — verify the DELIVERABLE. For any dispatch/queue/agent round-trip assert: (1) the input/`ref` payload actually reached the worker; (2) `result_bytes` is plausible and non-truncated (a round cap like 1024 is a tell), and the content actually answers the task; (3) any promised side-channel (issue comment, branch push, output file) actually landed. A status field is a CLAIM the system makes about its own lifecycle (an observation); the artifact is the evidence. This is the observation-vs-conclusion error applied to a status field: "item is `done`" is the observation, "the work succeeded" is the unverified conclusion.

class_hint: Fail-Loud — NFS transient mount failure marks container degraded
instance: Docker volume backed by NFS (`truenas:/mnt/zp1/ai-models`) occasionally returns "connection refused" at `docker compose up` time. The watcher's `applyPolicy()` catches the pull/start failure and enters `pull_failed_backoff` (300s). The host does not self-heal until the watcher is restarted or the backoff window expires. class_hint: Agent Coordination — Batch-dispatch of semi-related tasks produces N conflicting PRs
instance: Coordinator dispatches N individually-queued Codex issues for a batch of tasks in the same repo without grouping by file-area ownership. Codex picks them all up in parallel, opens N draft PRs simultaneously, and they conflict each other on shared files (e.g., docker-compose.yml, go flags files, docs). Root cause: parallel-safe check only catches exact file-path overlap in plan files, not "same file-area" overlap. A batch of OOBE fixes touching cmd/, deploy/, docs/ in one repo is effectively one logical unit dispatched as N separate units. Cost: N round-trips to Codex for rebases; wasted CI cycles; merge churn. Fix: (1) GROUP by file-area — bundle tasks that span the same repo+file-area into 1–3 issues by area (cmd/ fixes → one issue, deploy/ fixes → one issue, docs fixes → one issue); (2) if keeping separate issues, enforce strict sequence — remove parallel-safe from all but the first; each must merge before the next is dispatched; (3) never mark issues parallel-safe within the same repo batch unless file sets are truly disjoint (different packages, different service boundaries). Introduced: 2026-06-22 — factvault OOBE batch (issues #210–#217, 8 issues → 8 simultaneous PRs → 5 conflicts on first merge pass).

class_hint: Observability / Agent Coordination — Silent consumer death, no liveness/staleness alerting on dispatch pipeline
instance: The codex-attach consumer (Docker container codex-agent) died and stayed dead ~10 hours. Nothing alerted. The queue kept accepting enqueues; ~50 items dead-lettered silently, and GitHub issue labels stayed cosmetically `agent/codex/queued`. Discovered only by manual inspection after PRs sat idle. Root cause: no automated detection for "consumer alive but not consuming" or "consumer dead." Three missing detection layers: (1) Consumer liveness — no per-capability last-claim heartbeat + staleness alert; (2) Queue health — no alert on items queued > N min unclaimed, no dead-letter-rate alert (50 dead-letters accumulated with zero notification); (3) End-to-end canary — no scheduled synthetic item proving the pipeline completes work. Compounding: GitHub labels are cosmetic and lie (stay `queued`); the fleet-dispatch /items API is the only truth source for actual queue state. Cost: ~10h pipeline outage undetected; multiple false-start re-enqueues; manual diagnosis. Observed: 2026-06-23 — codex-agent container dead during factvault OOBE rebase cycle, items dead-lettered in silence.
check: (1) Per-capability liveness: alert when a capability has queued items but no consumer claim/heartbeat in 15 min. (2) Queue-health alerts: item-age threshold + dead-letter-rate spike alert. (3) Scheduled end-to-end canary (enqueue trivial no-op every ~10 min; alert if not completed within SLA) — catches ALL pipeline failure causes regardless of root cause. (4) Container-level: Docker healthcheck that probes the attach-loop liveness (not just process-exists) + autoheal sidecar for self-recovery; keep canary alerting so silent auto-restarts don't mask deeper faults. Tracked: fleet-dispatch#65 (canary + LAST_SUCCESS staleness) covers layers 1+3; fleet-dispatch#67 (structured harness logging) feeds the alerting. Prioritize #65 to p1 after this incident.

class_hint: Fail-Loud / Fleet-Dispatch — Fleet consumer silently not claiming: wrong-token default + gate-reset-on-deploy, no alerting
instance: Queued items for capability `impl-grok` sat indefinitely with `retries=0`, `lease_holder:""`. Consumer container healthy (uptime + healthcheck pass), fleet-dispatch server healthy, no error surfaced anywhere. Compound root causes: (1) `deploy-grok-machine.sh:~51` defaults `FLEET_TOKEN_FILE` to `token-impl` (Codex token) instead of `token-impl-grok`; server returns `{empty:true}` on every `/claim` because that token's `consumes` set lacks the target capability — silently; (2) `deploy-grok-machine.sh:~127` always writes `GROK_ATTACH_ENABLED=0`, disabling claiming on every redeploy regardless of prior state; (3) no alert fires on "items queued with no lease for N minutes" or "consumer token `consumes` does not include its target capability." Burned a multi-step diagnostic cycle (poll → k8s health → host docker → token-sha comparison) before isolating the cause. (Bug: petersimmons1972/claude-codex#316)
check: (a) Deploy default must use the capability-specific token (`token-impl-grok`), not the generic `token-impl`; validate at startup. (b) Persist gate state across redeploys, or make ENABLED the default post-cutover. (c) Consumer must log LOUDLY at startup when its token's `consumes` does not include the capability it was deployed to serve. (d) Alert on queue items with `lease_holder:""` older than N minutes and on a consumer whose token `consumes` is empty for its intended capability. Detection: `docker logs <consumer> --tail=25` → "standing by (disabled mode)" or empty-claim loops; compare token sha256 vs intended capability token; `GET /item/<id>` for persistent empty `lease_holder`.

class_hint: Fail-Loud / Infra / Config-Drift — Running container/config drifts from manifest: hand-edits and deploy resets diverge live state from source-of-truth, neither reconciles
instance: The live running container's effective config differs from what the declared manifest / deploy script / IaC source-of-truth would produce. Hand-fixes to the running host (sed-editing a live `.env`, `kubectl patch` on a secret) appear applied but are silently reverted on the next deploy or by ESO reconciliation; conversely, deploy scripts overwrite intended runtime state (e.g. resetting an enable gate to 0) on every run. "What's running" ≠ "what's declared," and nothing flags the gap. Root causes: (1) Deploy script writes authoritative values that overwrite operationally-critical runtime state on every redeploy (`deploy-grok-machine.sh:~127` forces `GROK_ATTACH_ENABLED=0`); (2) Operators hand-patch live state to work around it (sed on `.env`), creating drift the next deploy silently reverts; (3) ESO-managed k8s secrets (`fleet-dispatch-tokens`) have their source of truth in Infisical; direct `kubectl patch` looks applied but is reverted on next sync; (4) No drift detection comparing running effective config to the declared manifest / IaC source. Each layer (enable gate, consumer token, server-side `consumes` registration) gets patched at the LIVE container instead of at the source of truth, so it re-breaks on the next reconcile/deploy. Cost: this session — a hand-edited gate and a proposed k8s-secret patch would each have been reverted; compounded the FM-119 diagnostic chase. Related: FM-119, petersimmons1972/claude-codex#316.
check: After ANY deploy or ESO sync, diff the running container's effective env/config against (a) the deploy script's output and (b) the IaC source; re-verify runtime invariants (gate on, token identity, consumes set). Make every config change at the source of truth only — Infisical `ATTACH_TOKENS` for tokens/consumes (then force-sync + rollout-restart), the deploy script defaults / committed `.env` template for runtime flags — never hand-edit live state. Deploy scripts must PRESERVE operationally-critical state (don't hard-reset an enable gate). Add a reconcile/drift check (running vs declared) to the consumer healthcheck so divergence is loud, not silent.

class_hint: Deploy / Verify Discipline — live-deploy drift / running-ahead-of-manifest (extends FM-120)
instance: A running container or host-installed artifact is ahead of its source-of-truth: a `cp`/hand-edit applied to a live container without the identical change committed to source + image; a deployment rolled to an image tag the repo manifest does not pin; a `kubectl apply` of a change not yet on `main`. On the next rebuild, restart, or GitOps reconcile the running state silently regresses — symptom appears hours or days later with no clear cause. Observed: fleet-dispatch overnight runs #76/#78 (in-container `git pull`+`cp` of codex-poll NFF+lint patches); any `kubectl set image` outside a PR cycle.
check: (a) Manifest-first: before or simultaneously with any deploy, commit the change to source AND update the manifest/image so rebuild reproduces running state exactly. (b) After any deploy, run `~/bin/check-manifest-drift.sh` and assert PASS before closing the task. (c) Drift = wake-the-founder-class incident. Detection: automated CronJob `manifest-drift-check` in `ai-fleet` namespace (`aifleet/controller/deploy/manifest-drift-cronjob.yaml`, founder-gated apply). Manual check: `~/bin/check-manifest-drift.sh`.

class_hint: Infra / vLLM — Stale flag in docs causes crash-loop on cutover: `--disable-frontend-multiprocessing` removed in vLLM V1
instance: During Qwen2.5-72B production cutover on oblivion (2026-06-25), the new GPUHost CRD included `--disable-frontend-multiprocessing` based on `spark/docs/vllm-builds.md` which documented it as "required for stable GB10 operation." vLLM v0.20.0 (V1 engine) does not recognize this flag — `unrecognized arguments: --disable-frontend-multiprocessing`. The container crash-looped for ~3 min while the watcher kept recreating it. Root cause: the flag was valid in earlier vLLM versions where the frontend/backend were separate processes, but vLLM V1 merged the architecture. The running Nemotron config had never included this flag and worked fine — the docs introduced a stale claim that the plan incorporated without verifying against the existing working config.
check: (1) Before adding any vLLM flag from docs/notes to a new model config, verify the flag exists in the target version: `docker run --rm --entrypoint '' <image> python3 -c "import vllm; print(vllm.__version__)"` then compare against existing working configs for that image version. (2) When updating an existing model config, diff the proposed flags against the working config rather than starting from documentation. (3) `vllm-builds.md` entries for specific flags should include the vLLM version range they apply to. Detection: `docker logs <container> --tail=5` immediately after watcher starts the new container — `unrecognized arguments` exits within seconds. Fix: remove the flag from the CRD and reapply; watcher reconverges on next 60s poll cycle.

class_hint: Identity vs. Routing / Fail-Loud — duplicate consumer identity
instance: Two processes shared one token: a stale systemd `codex-attach.service` had been 401ing since 2026-06-25 alongside the container consumer. Its retry loop never exited, so `Restart=on-failure` never fired and systemd remained `active`; the unit also had no `WatchdogSec` or `OnFailure`. Observed in the 2026-07-03 audit ([claude-codex#362](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/claude-codex/issues/362)).
check: **Automated detection/alerting: none; manual signal: repeated 401 logs plus service/process inspection. Current mitigation: none.** Proposed: bind each distinct scoped credential to a stable consumer ID, reject a second concurrent session for that ID server-side, exit after a configured consecutive-401 threshold, and add systemd watchdog/failure notification.

class_hint: Delivery Durability / Fail-Loud — completed report discarded during Postgres outage
instance: A transient Postgres failure at report time can discard an otherwise completed LLM run: the Hermes consumer makes one `/report` attempt ([fleet-dispatch#133](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/fleet-dispatch/issues/133)), while Codex retries for only about 15 seconds. Structurally certain in the 2026-07-03 audit ([claude-codex#362](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/claude-codex/issues/362)).
check: **Durable lost-output/ack detection: none; a report-request failure may remain only in consumer logs. Current mitigation: partial only (Codex's approximately 15-second retry; none for Hermes).** Proposed: durably spool completed reports with restrictive permissions, bounded retention, and no secret-bearing logs; retry idempotently until acknowledged; alert and reconcile completed runs lacking an acknowledgement.

class_hint: Agent Coordination / Canary Integrity — no-consumer accumulation
instance: Canary items can enqueue indefinitely when no consumer claims their capability, so the canary certifies nothing while the queue grows ([fleet-dispatch#140](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/fleet-dispatch/issues/140)); identified in the 2026-07-03 audit ([claude-codex#362](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/claude-codex/issues/362)).
check: **Automated detection/alerting: none; manual signal: queued age and empty `lease_holder`. Current mitigation: none.** Proposed: fail enqueue when no authenticated, capability-authorized, fresh consumer registration exists; otherwise retain an auditable failed-canary result at the claim deadline and alert its owner.

class_hint: Fail-Loud / Observability — startup credential missing silent crash-loop
instance: In the opencode incident, an attach consumer crash-looped at startup because a required credential was missing. `ai-fleet-watcher` monitored model containers only, not attach consumers, so the failure was silent. The 2026-07-03 audit record ([claude-codex#362](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/claude-codex/issues/362)) is the sole incident reference supplied.
check: **Automated detection/alerting for attach consumers: none; manual signal: service/process restart inspection. Current mitigation: none.** Proposed: fail startup credential preflight loudly; alert the service owner on any preflight failure or crash loop and when the end-to-end attach canary exceeds its configured freshness interval.

class_hint: Deliverable Integrity / Semantic Validation — well-formed garbage accepted as `done`
instance: A `comment_only` report can be syntactically valid yet semantically empty and still reach `done`, because that lane has neither an artifact gate nor a semantic deliverable check; structurally certain at the `/report` acceptance boundary in the 2026-07-03 audit ([claude-codex#362](https://github.com/petersimmons1972/claude-codex/issues/362)).
check: **Automated semantic detection: none; manual signal: review the persisted `done` report. Current mitigation: none.** Proposed: reject terminal `done` unless the comment is non-empty, non-placeholder, and task-relevant; retain an explicit failed-validation state and cover the acceptance boundary with adversarial fixtures.

instance: 2026-08-06 fleet#268: a regression check for the fleet#265 plugin state-dir collision imported each installed plugin's state.mjs and compared resolved paths. With zero modules probing, the collision set was empty and the script printed 'PASS 2 plugins resolve to 0 distinct state paths' and exited 0 - a sentence that contradicts itself and still read green. The guarded failure is a plugin update overwriting state.mjs; a plugin update is also the most likely cause of a changed or missing export, so the update that reverts the fix is the update that silences the alarm. The check had passed BOTH validation arms (green on patched plugins, red on unpatched) before this was found by adversarial review - arm coverage proved the check works when it can see, and said nothing about what it does when it cannot. Fixed with a distinct exit code 3 'cannot certify' that forbids a pass whenever any target failed to probe [recurrence_of: none]
check: When a check inspects targets it must first load, enumerate or parse, ask what happens if loading FAILS for every target. If the check computes its verdict only over successfully-loaded targets, an all-fail run yields an empty result set, which reads as 'no violations found' and exits green. This is critical when the failure being guarded against is also the thing that breaks loading - then the guard's blind spot and its trigger are the SAME event, and the check goes silent at precisely the moment it is needed. A check must distinguish 'looked and found nothing' from 'could not look', and only the first may pass

check: A state document with an explicit BLOCKED section must have exactly one writer per subject. When a gate lifts, the ruling is typically recorded where the next actor is meant to start, and the now-false blocking entry is left in place because it was true when written -- so the document simultaneously says 'nothing is blocked, begin' and 'this is forbidden until he answers'. The two readings are not equally likely: a cautious agent checks the blocked list BEFORE acting, so the stale entry wins, and the correct behaviour of that agent is to stop and re-ask a question the founder has already answered -- converting a lifted gate back into founder attention, which is the exact cost the ruling was meant to end. Lifting a gate is a TWO-SITE edit: record the ruling and delete the entry it voids, in the same write. A staleness check that scans for banned words cannot catch this, because both sentences are well-formed and neither is individually stale-looking; the defect exists only in the relation between them

check: When a build loop stalls, ask which ARTIFACT each review round actually examined. A loop that reviews only the implementation can iterate indefinitely against a defective specification: each round the reviewer finds a real defect, the implementer fixes the coordinate named, and the next round finds the same class one coordinate over -- a pattern that reads as a careless implementer and is in fact a faithful one executing a wrong instruction. The tell is a defect traceable to a sentence in the spec rather than a line in the diff. The fix is to make the spec a reviewed artifact in its own right, adversarially, BEFORE any builder sees it, and to keep each accepted correction visibly IN the spec as a marked block, so the reasoning that produced the bad instruction is not rediscovered and reapplied by the next author

instance: 2026-08-07 fleet#191 PR #250 round 3, harness/archaeology.py. The round-3 brief said to stop a failed ledger-repair write from being swallowed: record the failure into state, which index() already drains. The implementer did exactly that, correctly, and _append_agent_rows then opened the same file and appended anyway, never consulting state['write_failures']. Measured: one valid row plus a blocked terminate-write produced a single unparseable 1795-byte line, TWO ROWS DESTROYED, while the run reported rows_written=1. Before the diff the OSError propagated and nothing was appended, so the row survived -- the fix made the failure mode strictly worse than the code it replaced. It does not self-heal, because the append re-terminates the file so it is no longer a torn FINAL line and every later run reports it permanently corrupt. Adversarial review classified it a blocker and the branch as worse than main for that damage class. The same session's round-4 spec review, briefed to read specs against code before any builder saw them, caught the identical omission class in a DIFFERENT spec of mine before implementation: 'the zero-new-rows path must read the ledger before returning' never said UNDER THE LOCK, and the early return sits before the lock acquisition, so a literal implementation with repair=True could truncate an unterminated final line while another process was mid-append -- verbatim what that lock's own docstring existed to prevent [recurrence_of: none]
check: When specifying a fix for a swallowed or ignored error, state the post-condition on the ARTIFACT -- the file, the row count, the bytes on disk, the instruction the operator receives -- never the internal step imagined to produce it. 'Record the failure into state, which the caller already drains' is satisfiable, faithfully and correctly, by code that records the damage and then proceeds to cause it. 'After any run in which a repair failed, the count of valid parseable rows in the file must be at least its pre-run count' is not. The asymmetry is that a bookkeeping instruction is satisfied by an observation, while a post-condition is satisfied only by an outcome. A second, sharper form of the same error: an ABORT path is frequently load-bearing precisely BECAUSE it does nothing. Repairing the abort so it reports properly can convert a data-preserving refusal into a data-destroying continue, which is strictly worse than the swallowed error it was written to fix. For any repair to an abort, ask what aborting used to protect and whether the new path still protects it

check: Reviewing the spec before the build works and has now paid twice, but a spec reviewer briefed only against the implementation has a blind spot exactly the size of the test suite. A new requirement can be internally sound, correctly scoped, and still contradict an assertion already committed in the suite -- and that contradiction is invisible to a reviewer reading the code. The failure surfaces late and in a shape that misdirects: a red suite at the end of an otherwise clean build round, on a test the implementer is correctly forbidden to touch, because a round scoped 'fix exactly these N defects and nothing else' rightly denies unilateral resolution of a spec conflict. Give the spec reviewer the test file as a second input, with the explicit instruction: for each new requirement, locate the existing assertions it touches and state whether any contradicts it. And handle the conflict as what it is -- a spec conflict is not a code defect. It needs one RULING from the spec author, and then a TEST AUTHOR makes the edit, never the implementer and never the coordinator. Which side wins is decided by asking what the fix exists to buy, not by which text is older

instance: Session tried to reconcile a divergence in ONE file (notes/backlog.md) between local main and origin/main by running 'git reset --soft origin/main' (intending only to move HEAD so a subsequent narrow commit would apply cleanly). --soft does not touch the index or working tree -- both remained at the OLD, stale local main's state, which was itself significantly behind the true origin/main (many files had been added/removed upstream via commits local main never had). The subsequent 'git add <one-file> && git commit' committed not just that file but the entire pre-existing stale-index-vs-new-HEAD diff, since nothing had reset the index/working tree to match the new HEAD. Force-pushed without independently diffing old-remote-tip vs new-commit first -- the deletion of 935 lines (a real test file) plus ~5 other files and several stale script reversions went unnoticed until directly asked to audit the pushed commit's contents. Caught only by comparing the actual pre-push remote tip against the new commit's tree file-by-file, not by the diff --stat summary alone (that showed 99 files changed but wasn't inspected line-by-line before push). Fix used: git switch -C <branch> <real-pre-push-tip> (clean re-checkout, not --soft), reapply ONLY the intended diff via a plain append/patch, verify 'git status --short' shows exactly one file before committing, verify the new commit's diff against the pre-push tip shows only the intended change, THEN push. General rule: before pushing any commit produced by 'reset --soft' + partial 'add', diff the new commit against the immediate parent and confirm the file list matches intent exactly -- do not trust a bare 'files changed' count. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #none)

instance: Measured 2026-08-15/16 (session 817d0e1f, CI-fleet audit): ~/.bash_env minted the Claude GitHub App installation token unconditionally on every non-interactive bash startup, so Codex-harness and Grok-harness processes inherited GH_TOKEN and authenticated to GitHub AS psimmons-claude-worker[bot]. Every commit, comment and API call they made was attributed to another harness, silently destroying the per-harness attribution that independent-review routing depends on (an agent could not tell it was borrowing an identity because gh auth status showed a valid App token). Detection: compare the acting bot login in a GitHub event against the harness that produced it; a single harness login across all harnesses is proof. Fix applied: route the mint on harness detection with default-deny (no harness detected = no token) rather than a single hardcoded harness. Related family: FM-292 (background/cron sessions falling through to founder OAuth) - same root surface (~/.bash_env + PROMPT_COMMAND refresh), different failure direction: FM-292 loses the App identity downward to OAuth, this one imposes ONE harness identity sideways onto all others. [recurrence_of: none]
check: A shared credential-mint path must select the credential by DETECTED HARNESS with default-deny, never mint one harness credential unconditionally for every shell

instance: Measured 2026-08-15/16 (session 817d0e1f). cli-dispatch line 5931 advises operators and agents to retry with `env -u GH_TOKEN gh ...` when an App-token call returns 401. That silently swaps the GitHub App identity for the founder personal OAuth identity: the call then succeeds, so nothing looks wrong, while attribution moves to a human and the personal 5000/hr quota absorbs fleet traffic. Filed as fleet#546. The failure is not that an agent broke a rule - the rule (App tokens exclusively) was correctly recorded and repeatedly restated - it is that the TOOL taught the violation at exactly the moment of failure, when an agent is most likely to follow instructions verbatim. General check: grep tooling error paths and docs for remediation advice that removes a credential, lowers a permission, disables a check, or skips a gate; that advice is a defect, not documentation. Related: FM-292 records the same advice as one compounding cause of the 6th recurrence of OAuth quota starvation; this entry isolates the pattern so it is findable outside the GitHub-auth context. [recurrence_of: none]
check: A tool must never document a fallback that downgrades identity or authority as the remedy for its own auth error; remediation text inside tooling is an instruction, and it will be followed

instance: Measured 2026-08-15/16 (session 817d0e1f, CI-fleet audit). A coordinator brief listed a KNOWN FACTS block; three of its entries were false and the executing agents spent budget falsifying them instead of doing the assigned work: (1) "armies CI has been failing for 4 months" - it had not; (2) "fleet-sync targets 404 because the repos were deleted" - they had been TRANSFERRED, not deleted; (3) "the telemetry units are instinct-project detritus" - zero overlap with instinct. One of the wrong root causes was published to fleet#549 before correction, so the error escaped the session into a public issue. Cost shape: a wrong fact in a brief is worse than an absent one, because the agent trusts it and reasons FORWARD from it, and the correction arrives only if the agent happens to trip over ground truth. Check: in any brief, each factual claim carries a command or artifact reference the executor can re-run in one step, or it is written as "unverified - confirm first". [recurrence_of: none]
check: A dispatch brief may not present unverified premises as KNOWN FACTS; every asserted fact in a brief is either carried with its verifying artifact or labelled a hypothesis to test

instance: Measured 2026-08-15/16 (session 817d0e1f). ~/HANDOFF.md - a file this session read at startup - already carried an entry from the fleet#405 work recording that Claude had personally authored every fix instead of dispatching Codex, violating the standing "Claude is QA, not builder" ruling. In this session I again personally authored the merge-gate fixes in ~/.claude/workflows (commits d407cfa, 4b05bf6, ffcd8ae, 0a4270f) rather than dispatching a builder. The prior occurrence was in context, in a file loaded before any work began, describing exactly the act about to be repeated. This is the same shape as FM-277 (an agent leaked a token while holding FM-96 in context) and cluster c-018: preloaded warnings have a measured miss rate near 100% at the moment of action, because the agent is attending to the task, not the registry. Check: for any rule of the form "role X must not do Y", place a mechanical gate at the point of action (a dispatch precondition, a pre-commit author check, a workflow step that refuses) - counting on the rule being loaded is not a control. [recurrence_of: c-018]
check: A failure mode recorded in an always-loaded file does not prevent its own recurrence; the standing rule it encodes must be enforced by a runtime gate or a dispatch-time check, not by being read

instance: Measured 2026-08-15/16 (session 817d0e1f). Four merge-gate defects in ~/.claude/workflows were each proven by a discriminating test run by hand: pev.js returned MERGE on 0/3 lenses before d407cfa and BLOCKED after; pr-whole.js returned MERGE-READY on 0/3 lenses before 4b05bf6; tdd-build.js accepted a self-reported PASS before ffcd8ae; unit.js/lib/converge.js accepted non-executed acceptance evidence before 0a4270f. Every one of those tests exists only as a transcript command. ~/.claude/workflows has no CI, no pre-commit hook, and no test runner, so the next edit to pev.js can silently reinstate the vacuous-quantifier bug and nothing anywhere will notice - the proof does not survive the session that produced it. This is the concrete form of "enforce in runtime, not policy": the code was fixed and the ENFORCEMENT was not, and only the enforcement is what makes the fix durable. Check: for every fix, name the automatic path that will re-run its discriminating test; if the answer is "I ran it", the item is not done. [recurrence_of: none]
check: A defect proven fixed by a hand-run discriminating test is not closed until that test runs in an automatic path; an unwired proof expires the moment the session ends

instance: Measured 2026-08-15/16 (session 817d0e1f), two independent instances in one session, both caught only because the executing agent overruled the brief. (1) I instructed an agent to verify workflow-script integrity with `node --check`; on files that mix ES-module export with a top-level return, node --check exits 0 even with `const x = (((;` appended - the prescribed method cannot fail, so it would have certified corrupted files (FM-287). (2) I specified measuring CI queue delay at RUN level; GitHub sets run_started_at ~= created_at, making run-level queue delay identically zero by construction, which would have inverted the ARC runner-sizing conclusion to "no warm pools needed" (FM-291). In both cases the QUESTION was sound and the METHOD was vacuous, and the vacuity was invisible to the author precisely because he chose the method for its plausibility. Checks: (a) briefs state the question plus what a PASS and a FAIL must each look like, leaving method to the executor; (b) any prescribed method ships with a positive control - show the method failing on a known-bad input before trusting it on the real one; (c) executors are told explicitly that overruling a method whose blind spot they can demonstrate is expected behaviour, not scope creep. [recurrence_of: none]
check: A brief must specify the QUESTION and its acceptance criterion, not the verification METHOD; a coordinator-chosen method carries a blind spot the coordinator cannot see, and the executor must be authorised to overrule it

instance: fleet PR #558: cmd_acceptance stripped */cli-dispatch-bg-guard.* from PATH so run_one_check would resolve the real setsid, but BACKGROUND_GUARD_DIR was unset in the fresh process, so item commands also got real setsid/nohup. PoC: --item "esc=setsid bash -c 'sleep 19; echo leaked' &" returned {"exit_code":0} while the work kept running in a new session/pgid; bg_reap_process_group only reaps the check's own pgid. A false zero in the very mechanism that decides whether anything is green. In-group nohup was correctly refused with 45, which is what made the escape look safe. Found by cross-vendor review (Grok) after CI green and coordinator-executed acceptance both passed. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #547)
check: An acceptance runner that strips a background-guard shim from PATH must re-arm the guard for the ITEM command, or genuinely backgrounded work escapes refusal and reports exit 0

instance: fleet #560: a --harness grok review lane posted its VERDICT comment as psimmons-claude-worker. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #560)

instance: fleet PR #557: a detector banning mis-cited calibration figures used GROUP_RE = digits separated by bare slashes. The repo's own gate comments write '11 / 17 / 23' with spaces, so re-inserting the verbatim pre-fix sentences in house style passed clean -- a one-character style change restored the bug under a green suite. Its equivalence rule banned only 'exact'/'identical', so 'the same numbers as' and 'is equivalent to' laundered the identical claim. A synonym blacklist keeps losing this race; inverting the rule (any non-registered figure in a linkvault sentence is a violation unless it is a pure self-description) is the durable shape. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #516)

Three improvised different routes to the PR head (isolated archive, git archive/show, temp clone at /tmp) and one refused outright because git rev-parse HEAD returned the base. [recurrence_of: none]

instance: fleet PR #558 closed the setsid process-group escape by arming the background guard for the item command, verified: --item "esc=setsid ... &" went from exit_code 0 with a live orphan to 45 with none. But the guard works by shimming PATH lookups, so /usr/bin/setsid still escapes and still reports exit_code 0. Correctly judged a pre-existing limit of run_one_check rather than a regression, so the PR merged -- but it leaves a live false zero in the mechanism that now decides whether anything is green. Durable fix is a post-execution check that no descendant session survived, not an enumeration of detacher names, which loses the same race a synonym blacklist does. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #547)
check: A guard implemented by shimming PATH catches only the idiomatic invocation; an absolute-path call bypasses it entirely

instance: A dispatch acceptance gate resolved the tree under test as REPO=${1:-/home/psimmons/projects/fleet}. cli-dispatch stages the check script OUTSIDE the worktree and invokes it with NO argument, so the default won every in-lane run and the gate inspected the coordinator's UNFIXED main checkout rather than the agent's worktree. The gate reported check-failed for a CORRECT implementation twice in a row (fleet#540 attempt 1 and its retry); those two failures looked like a same-class IMPLEMENTATION failure and would have triggered a vendor switch under the loop cap, spending a second lane to re-fail against the same broken gate. Verified directly: with the worktree passed as an argument the script exits 0; with no argument, from inside that worktree, it exits 1 at the first probe. The implementation satisfied the positive control, all 8 direct behaviour probes, and 21 bats cases. SIGNATURE: a check runnable BOTH by a coordinator and inside a lane must resolve its target from its own cwd, never a default path, and must refuse loudly with a distinct non-zero exit when it cannot locate the tree - a gate that cannot find its own tree must never be able to report a pass. The direction here was fail-CLOSED, the only reason it was survivable; the identical defect in a gate whose default tree already satisfies the property fails OPEN and silently passes every broken implementation. DIAGNOSTIC LESSON: two consecutive same-class lane failures must be classified impl-caused vs gate-caused BEFORE the loop cap's method change is applied, because the cap's prescribed remedy (switch vendor) is exactly wrong for a gate-caused failure. Second occurrence of this shape in one session - the same hardcoded-path defect was caught pre-dispatch in the fleet#516 adversarial probe, where it would have made a lane test the coordinator's tree instead of its own. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #540)
check: Acceptance gate defaults to a hardcoded checkout, so every in-lane run tests the coordinator's tree instead of the agent's

instance: A coordinator brief told a verifier to prove a new contract test guards a vendor patch by reverting the patch and running: ./dispatch/test/run-suite.sh --filter codex-evidence dispatch/test/codex-evidence-contract.bats -- expecting a non-zero exit as proof the guard fires. bats --filter matches TEST NAMES, not files, and no test in that file is named 'codex-evidence', so the filter selected ZERO tests and the runner exited 1 unconditionally. The command therefore returns 'guard fired' whether the guard works, is broken, or does not exist - the intended RED and the vacuous RED are indistinguishable. Confirmed directly afterward: FILTER_EXIT=1 with zero cases selected. The verifier noticed the mismatch and substituted a real proof (revert to the pre-patch backup, observe 4 specific red cases fail while both positive controls still pass), which is the only reason a vacuous result was not banked as evidence that the fleet-owned half of the item was sound. SIGNATURE: a check whose FAILURE mode is indistinguishable from its SUCCESS mode proves nothing, and a selector that silently matches nothing is the commonest way to build one. Any command used as proof-of-red must first be shown to select a non-empty set, and must be distinguishable from the empty-selection case - print the selected count, or assert the expected number of executed cases, never just the exit code. Same family as a green suite whose assertions never ran: the exit code is trusted while the population it ran over is unexamined. Note the direction: this one fails CLOSED into a FALSE POSITIVE - it manufactures evidence that a guard works, which is more dangerous than a missed defect because it terminates further checking. [recurrence_of: none]
check: Verification command in a dispatch brief was unsatisfiable, so it would have 'proved' the guard works regardless of truth

instance: fleet#540: acceptance gate green, but ./dispatch/test/run-suite.sh --jobs 4 gave HEAD EXIT=1 CASES=1601 FAILED=1 against BASE EXIT=0 CASES=1598 FAILED=0. The count went UP by 3 because the change added tests, while a DIFFERENT pre-existing test broke. The campaign's standard floor 'executed count >= base' is satisfied (1601 >= 1598) and therefore blind: it can only detect deletion of cases, never breakage of them. Only the runner EXIT CODE and the not-ok count caught it. The broken test was 'audition: the per-root lock does not suppress a protected transaction failure' (lifecycle-lock-scope.bats:271): audition_with_record_lock began swallowing a non-zero status from the function it protects, so a failed transaction reported success to its caller - a false green inside a lock wrapper that many callers inherit. SIGNATURE: count-based conservation checks and pass/fail checks are ORTHOGONAL and neither substitutes for the other; a PR that adds tests can hide a regression from a count floor indefinitely. Any gate asserting 'count >= base' must ALSO assert exit==0 and failed==0 at both commits, and must report all four numbers. Second-order lesson: the acceptance gate ran only the 21-case file the feature touched and was green, so a gate passing is not a suite passing - scope the acceptance run to the whole suite before merge, not to the feature's own file. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #540)
check: Full suite fails while the executed-case count INCREASES, so a count-vs-base floor sees no regression

instance: fleet#566: tests/test_static_calibration_gate.py verifies 'if data/task-calibration.jsonl has a row for this hash, it must match live scores'. The hash is computed over the task TREE, so ANY edit inside the task tree changes the hash, removes the matching row, and makes the check SKIP rather than fail - 'skipped: registry has no row for current linkvault hash yet'. Demonstrated with a PURE COMMENT change (fixing two stale fixture docstrings): before the edit 'Ran 94 tests / OK', after 'Ran 94 tests / OK (skipped=1)'. Verified both directions by stashing the edit and re-running. The executed-case count is IDENTICAL at 94, so a count-vs-base floor cannot see the disarming either. The check exists to catch a task tree drifting from its registered calibration, and the mechanism that signals drift is the mechanism that suppresses the check - a real logic change moving the floor from 13 would produce the identical green. SIGNATURE: absence of a lookup key must not be inferred as 'nothing to check'; absence is also exactly what a regression looks like. A check that cannot evaluate its predicate must FAIL, with a distinct signal, never skip. If a legitimate state genuinely lacks the key (a brand-new task before first calibration) that state must be represented EXPLICITLY - a marker, an allowlist, a 'pending' band - never inferred from absence. Near-identical prior art in this corpus: hc-FM-217, where modules that failed to import were collected into an 'unresolved' warn list and excluded from the comparison, leaving an empty collision set that printed PASS. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #566)
check: Consistency check SKIPS when its lookup key is absent, so the very edit it polices disarms it

instance: fleet#516/#565: a guard against citing the wrong calibration gate went through four build rounds, each reviewed by an independent cross-vendor reviewer, each shipping GREEN and each bypassed a different way. R1/R2 were a blacklist of phrasings (any natural rewrite slipped past; cap hit, method changed). R3 inverted the rule to deny-by-default with a small permit set, but the permit test compared value MEMBERSHIP not shape, so 13/13/13 duplicated, 18/13 truncated and 23/18/13 reordered all passed. R4 compared exact shape/order/cardinality - and 13/18/23/29 then produced ZERO citation groups, because GROUP_RE's {1,2} quantifier plus a (?![\w/]) lookahead means an overlong run matches nothing at all. Critically 11/17/23/29 - the ORIGINAL WRONG GATE with a fourth value appended - became invisible: not permitted-too-generously, but never surfaced to the permit logic at all. SIGNATURE: every round hardened the JUDGE while leaving the RECOGNIZER narrow, and a candidate the recognizer never emits cannot be judged by any rule however strict. When successive fixes to a validator keep failing in NEW ways rather than repeating, suspect the extraction/tokenization stage rather than the decision stage: widen recognition FIRST, then tighten permits. Process lesson: a declared stopping rule set BEFORE the round (split the PR rather than run round five) is what stopped the loop; the verified factual correction was landed separately and the unconverged guard moved to its own issue rather than holding it hostage. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #565)
check: Four fix rounds each tightened the comparison while the tokenizer stayed narrow, so the bypass just moved

instance: fleet PR#564: an independent reviewer returned VERDICT fail with a HIGH finding that routing/README.md:79 cited '0-of-2 = 11/23, 1-of-2 = 17/23' for r3-linkvault-v1 and must be corrected to 13/18/23 to match the registered gate. Measured live rather than argued: static_calibration.py reports the FIXTURES score 13/18/23, so the registry half of the finding was right - but that documentation line describes OBSERVED MODEL SCORES, not the fixture calibration gradient. It is immediately followed by 'Measured actor profile (n=6/cell...)' and its bullets bind 11 and 17 to named model families, corroborated by the round-3 evidence FINDINGS.md. Applying the requested fix would have replaced a TRUE statement about what models scored with a FALSE one. SIGNATURE: two semantically different claims that share a numeric signature (here a 3-value gradient) will be conflated by a reviewer pattern-matching on the numbers, and the resulting correction is an OVER-correction - strictly worse than the miss, because it manufactures a fresh falsehood inside a document whose purpose is evidence, and it arrives wearing the authority of a review. Mitigation that worked: refuse to act on any citation finding until the claim TYPE is established by measurement, and dispatch a second independent reviewer explicitly tasked with attacking the refutation rather than re-reviewing the diff, since the party who wrote the refutation must not be the party who closes it out. Note the same review's MEDIUM finding was real and led to hc-FM for fleet#566 - a wrong headline finding is not a worthless review. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #564)
check: Reviewer conflated two distinct claims sharing a numeric signature and filed a HIGH that would have INTRODUCED an error

instance: A founder ruling (2026-08-16) changed the delivery contract for third-party changes: agents must commit a PATCH FILE into the repo instead of live-editing an installed plugin. The rework brief was updated accordingly and the lane complied exactly - it delivered dispatch/vendor-patches/codex-1.0.6-fleet-263.patch plus 498 lines of bats and left the installed plugin untouched, verified by mtime. But the ACCEPTANCE GATE was not updated: it still probed the INSTALLED plugin root. So it reported check-failed on all four fail-open probes, and its own summary line said 'NOT enforced by the installed plugin' - accurate about the thing it looked at, and irrelevant to the thing that was delivered. A perfectly compliant lane was scored as a failure, and the harness would have scored every future compliant lane the same way. SIGNATURE: an acceptance gate is one half of a delivery CONTRACT; changing what the producer emits without changing what the checker consumes leaves the checker silently validating the wrong artifact. Whenever a brief's deliverable shape changes - file instead of in-place edit, patch instead of commit, artifact instead of side effect - the gate must be re-pointed in the SAME change, and its discrimination re-proved against the new artifact. Note the failure direction: this one failed CLOSED (a good lane looked bad), which is survivable and self-announcing. The mirror case is a gate still pointed at a location where the property already holds, which fails OPEN and passes every broken lane silently. Third gate defect of this session in the same family - see the hardcoded-checkout gate and the unsatisfiable proof-of-red; the recurring root is that gates were written against an assumed artifact location and never re-verified against the real one. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #263)
check: Changing what a lane DELIVERS invalidated the gate that CONSUMES it, so the gate failed every compliant lane

instance: fleet PR#548 carried a parked disposition recording (a) a hold because it 'depends on fleet#386 by its own issue text' and (b) a fail-open-validator blocker marked SAME_CLASS_REPEAT, which under the loop cap forbids a third same-method attempt. Re-adjudicated at the unchanged head 5ecd9aa on 2026-08-16: BOTH were false. #386 had CLOSED on 2026-08-10, satisfying the dependency. The fail-open blocker was not reproducible - every gate the PR names fails CLOSED when starved: absent input -> jq -e exit 2 and sha256sum -c exit 1; empty -> exit 4 / exit 1; malformed -> exit 5 / exit 1 / run_cmd exact-match exit 97. Because a SAME_CLASS_REPEAT verdict forbids re-attempt, the stale park was self-sealing: the very disposition that was wrong was also the reason nobody would re-test it, so it would have frozen the work indefinitely. The real blocker was something the park had never identified at all (see below). SIGNATURE: a parked disposition is a CLAIM WITH A TIMESTAMP, not a standing fact - it is evidence about a head at a moment, and both the world (dependencies closing) and the code can move underneath it. Re-verify a park before acting on it, in BOTH directions: it can be too pessimistic (blocking landable work) as well as too optimistic. The danger is asymmetric for terminal-sounding labels like SAME_CLASS_REPEAT, PARKED or REFUTE, which suppress the re-testing that would expose them; those need an explicit expiry or a re-verify-before-citing rule. Corollary observed in the same adjudication: parked dispositions record the blocker that was FOUND, not the blocker that MATTERS, so re-adjudication must re-derive from acceptance criteria rather than only re-checking the recorded findings. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #548)
check: A parked PR disposition rotted in BOTH directions and would have frozen the work indefinitely on an expired premise

instance: A dispatch lane live-edited an installed plugin outside its repo. The coordinator backed up the modified files, later restored from that backup, compared md5sums, saw them match, and reported 'plugin restored, md5-verified / installed plugin unchanged' - repeatedly and confidently, to the founder. The comparison was structurally incapable of showing what was claimed: the backup was taken AFTER the modification, so backup == installed proves only that the state was STABLE between the two reads, never that it was PRISTINE. Measured: vendor git HEAD 88d8dee vs backup 9f12e7b vs installed 9f12e7b - backup and installed agreed with each other and BOTH differed from the only provenance-bearing baseline. An independent reviewer caught it while checking an unrelated scope rule; the coordinator's own repeated verification never could have. Compounding error: the backup covered only the files that session happened to touch, not the full diff-vs-baseline, so a third modified file (codex-companion.mjs, carrying a DIFFERENT closed issue's live fix) was never snapshotted and was nearly destroyed by the obvious remediation. SIGNATURE: a restore/integrity check must compare against a PROVENANCE-BEARING baseline - git HEAD, a package checksum, a signed artifact, an upstream re-download - never against a snapshot derived from the artifact under test. Snapshot-vs-snapshot answers 'did it change since I looked?' and is routinely misread as 'is it as it should be?'. Determine the backup's provenance BEFORE trusting it as a restore point, and define the backup set from the full diff against the baseline, not from the subset you believe you modified. Same family as verifying a config against its documentation rather than against the running system. [recurrence_of: none] (GitHub #570)
check: Restore verified against a snapshot taken FROM the modified thing, proving stability and mistaken for pristineness

instance: Across one campaign session the coordinator dispatched build lanes with cli-dispatch start and omitted --no-pr three times (fleet #567, #571, #572). Each lane opened its own PR on its dispatch/<task> branch as soon as it delivered, before the coordinator had verified anything. All three had to be closed as duplicates of the PR the coordinator opened deliberately, and each duplicate carried a commit authored cli-dispatch@localhost, which resolves to NO GitHub login and therefore could never have landed anyway (cli-dispatch land refuses exit 27 when it cannot determine the authoring login). Consequences beyond the noise: an open PR is a claim that work is ready for review, so three unreviewed lane outputs sat publicly labelled as proposals; and a reviewer or a queue-draining workflow could have adjudicated the duplicate instead of the real PR, wasting a full review round on a branch nobody intended to merge. SIGNATURE: a dispatch tool whose DEFAULT is to publish means every omitted suppression flag is an outbound action taken without a decision. When the coordinator intends to open the PR itself after verification, --no-pr is not optional decoration; it is what keeps publication gated on the verification step. Fix at the dispatch site, not by remembering: put --no-pr in the standing build-lane invocation template alongside --check-script and --check-strength, so omitting it is a visible deletion rather than a silent default. Same family as any tool that treats publication as the default rather than an explicit act. [recurrence_of: none]
